name: flock_convergence_quality
content:
# Measuring Quality-of-Consensus: Small-Model Flock vs. Strong Remote Model

## 1. Framing: separate the three claims people conflate

"Consensus beats strong judgment" is actually three different claims, and each needs its own measurement:

1. **Raw quality claim**: flock-aggregated output is more accurate than one strong-model call.
2. **Risk-adjusted claim**: flock consensus gives better *selective* accuracy (it knows when it doesn't know), enabling abstention/cascades.
3. **Systems claim**: at matched cost/latency/failure-tolerance, the flock Pareto-dominates.

Most demos fail because they test only #1 with mismatched budgets. The framework below measures all three and produces a quantitative decision rule.

---

## 2. Workload suite (stratified by where theory predicts different outcomes)

Build 5–6 workload families, mixing public benchmarks with **real production traffic** (logged queries from an actual deployment, stratified):

| Family | Examples | Why included |
|---|---|---|
| Verifiable discrete | GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval+/execution-checked code, TriviaQA | Clean voting semantics; unambiguous grading |
| Classification/selection | MMLU, routing decisions, safety labels | Pure Condorcet regime |
| Free-form generation | Summarization, writing, open QA | Where naive voting breaks; forces MBR/judge designs |
| Agentic/sequential | Multi-step tool-use traces | Errors compound; per-step consensus may not help |
| Calibration-critical | Risk scoring, moderation | Joint-miss probability is the real metric |
| **Contamination-free slice** | Problems authored after model cutoffs, private repo tickets, date-stamped generated variants | Trust anchor immune to benchmark leakage |

For every family: 2,000–5,000 items (power analysis below), plus a 300–500-item human-double-annotated subset for open-ended grading validation (require grader–human κ ≥ 0.8 before trusting model graders).

---

## 3. Systems under test and the budget-matching discipline

**Flock side** — pool of ≥20 small models spanning families, sizes, and providers. Test multiple aggregators, because "consensus" is not one thing:

- Cross-model majority vote (n ∈ {3, 5, 7, 11})
- Within-model self-consistency (k samples, one small model) — isolates sampling diversity from model diversity
- Weighted vote (dev-set weights or logprob-weighted)
- MBR decoding (pick candidate maximizing average utility to others — required for free-form)
- Debate-then-vote (measure convergence rate and **sycophancy drift**: per-member accuracy before vs. after exposure to peers)
- **Cascade**: flock answers; defer to strong model only on disagreement/low agreement

**Strong side** — three baselines, not one:
1. Single greedy call
2. **Strong-model self-consistency at matched budget** ← the control almost everyone skips; much of the flock's advantage evaporates here
3. Distilled-small-model (the alternative way to spend the same money)

**Budget matching**: define cost in $/item (log every call's tokens and price). Sweep budget; report accuracy-vs-budget curves for all systems. Any "consensus wins" claim must hold at a matched point on the curve. Also track p50/p95 latency under realistic concurrency (parallel flock calls contend for rate limits — measure end-to-end, not per-call).

---

## 4. Metric suite

### A. Outcome quality
- Accuracy per workload with paired-bootstrap CIs (over items **and** over flock compositions)
- Accuracy at fixed budget multiples {1×, 3×, 10×} of strong-single-call price
- Tail behavior: accuracy on hardest decile; P(fail | difficult item)

### B. Consensus-process quality (the core novel measurements)

**Error correlation structure.** For members i, j estimate the phi coefficient on correctness indicators:

φ_ij = (P(both wrong) − q_i·q_j) / √(q_i(1−q_i)·q_j(1−q_j)),  q = error rate

Average over pairs → ρ_e. Estimate on medium/hard slices only (on easy items errors are too rare for stable estimates). This single number largely determines whether consensus can work.

**Predictive model (beta-binomial).** With exchangeable members, error rate q̄, and equicorrelated errors, the number of errors is Beta-Binomial(n, α, β) with α+β = (1−ρ_e)/ρ_e, α = q̄(1−ρ_e)/ρ_e. Then:

P(majority wrong) = P(X ≥ ⌈n/2⌉), X ~ BB(n, α, β)

This lets you *predict* flock accuracy from cheaply-measured (q̄, ρ_e, n) before running the full study — use it as a screening tool, then validate.

**Worked example** (members at p = 0.70, n = 7):

| ρ_e | Independent-case accuracy | Predicted majority accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| 0.0 | 87.4% | 87.4% |
| 0.1 | — | ~82% |
| 0.3 | — | ~75.5% |
| 0.5 | — | ~72% |

To beat a 90% strong model with 70%-accurate members you need roughly n ≈ 30+ at ρ_e ≈ 0.05 — feasible only if small-model calls are ≥30× cheaper. **This is the honest math for why flocks rarely win raw accuracy against frontier models; they win on cost-adjusted, selective, and robustness grounds.**

**Common-mode failure rate**: P(all members wrong) and P(all wrong | ≥1 wrong). In safety/moderation contexts this is *the* metric — two models both missing a violation is the dangerous event.

**Agreement-as-confidence**: fit P(correct | k of n agree) on dev; report AUROC of agreement predicting correctness, and compare to the strong model's self-reported confidence AUROC. If agreement-AUROC > confidence-AUROC, the flock gives you a better abstention signal than the strong model's own introspection.

**Selective prediction**: risk–coverage curves for (flock + abstain-on-disagreement) vs. (strong + confidence threshold). Report AURC. This is typically where flocks produce their clearest win.

**Oracle gaps**: majority-of-flock vs. oracle-any-member; strong-single vs. oracle-best-of-k. Large gaps = headroom for learned routing/selection rather than better members.

**Naive-vs-learned aggregation gap**: majority vote vs. stacked/weighted aggregator trained on dev. The gap quantifies how much signal naive consensus leaves on the table (minority-being-right rate).

**Fragility**:
- Composition variance: resample 100–200 random flocks from the pool; report std/min/max of accuracy (never report one composition)
- Paraphrase flip rate: consensus answer flip rate under prompt perturbation vs. strong model's flip rate
- Leave-one-out volatility; graceful-degradation curve (accuracy vs. members dropped, simulating outages)

### C. Economics and robustness
- $/item, tokens (in/out separately), p50/p95 latency, energy if relevant
- Degradation under member loss, rate-limiting, latency jitter (flock degrades gracefully; single strong model has cliff risk)
- Contamination audit: canary strings, n-gram overlap, and weight on the post-cutoff slice

---

## 5. Statistical machinery

- **Paired design**: same items to all systems; McNemar for binary outcomes; paired bootstrap for continuous scores
- **Power**: paired with ~5% discordance, n = 2,000 detects ~1.5–2pt gaps at 80% power; unpaired needs ~3k items for 3pt gaps. Plan 2–5k items per family
- **Multiple comparisons**: Benjamini–Hochberg across workload×metric cells; pre-register the primary metric (e.g., "accuracy at $X/item" and "AURC") per family
- **Per-slice analysis**: stratify by difficulty, topic cluster (embeddings), length, language; report per-slice deltas with empirical-Bayes shrinkage to avoid noise-chasing
- **Temperature ablation**: separate diversity-from-sampling from diversity-from-model-heterogeneity

---

## 6. When consensus actually wins — the tested hypotheses

**Flock favored when:**
1. Members are individually decent (>60–65%) and errors are **decorrelated** (ρ_e ≲ 0.2–0.3). Decorrelation levers: heterogeneous model families, different retrieval corpora/tools, varied personas/prompts, deliberately included dissenter members.
2. Answer space is discrete/verifiable — voting is well-defined.
3. Difficulty is heterogeneous and agreement is informative → cascades capture the win ("flock handles 80% of traffic, strong model handles the hard 20%, total cost 0.3–0.4× at equal accuracy" is the realistic headline result).
4. The task is stochastic (long CoT branching, many valid implementations) — pure variance reduction.
5. Requirements include tail control, abstention, redundancy against outages, or resistance to single-stack-targeted attacks.
6. Price ratio (strong : small) exceeds ~n×, making brute-force ensembling economical.

**Strong model favored when:**
1. Errors are correlated (shared training-data biases, universal reasoning traps) — measure P(all wrong | any wrong); if high, voting cancels nothing.
2. Capability gap is large: members near or below chance on the slice actively hurt (Condorcet requires p > 0.5 *and* independence).
3. Output is free-form/creative: voting degenerates, MBR mode-seeks into blandness (measure distinctness/self-BLEU alongside win-rate), judge-arbiters inject their own bias.
4. Sequential agentic tasks: per-step consensus doesn't fix trajectory divergence and multiplies cost.
5. Strict single-call latency SLOs with large outputs.
6. **The strong model buys the same ensembling**: strong-model self-consistency at matched budget closes most of the gap on many benchmarks — always run this control.

**Deployment-pattern conclusions the study should produce:**
- High-volume discrete tasks → flock vote + cascade to strong on disagreement (usually the actual winner)
- Hard reasoning → strong model, optionally with flock as a *critique/verification panel* (measure P(≥1 member flags | strong wrong) vs. false-alarm rate — checking is parallelizable even when generation isn't)
- Open-ended creation → strong single generator; flock repurposed as *evaluator* panel (consensus for grading, not generating)
- Safety-critical → flock for detection redundancy (minimize joint-miss), strong for resolution

---

## 7. Pitfalls checklist

1. Budget mismatch (flock-of-10 vs. one call) — fatal to validity
2. Missing the strong-model self-consistency control
3. Single flock composition reported as *the* flock
4. Judge bias: grading open-ended outputs with a competitor model — use blind pairwise with position-swapping, multiple graders, human anchors
5. Correlation estimated on easy items (range restriction)
6. Tie-breaking and answer-extraction losses ignored in voting pipelines
7. Naive latency math ignoring rate limits and concurrency
8. Benchmark contamination inflating the strong model — hence the post-cutoff slice as anchor

---

## 8. Minimal viable version (2 weeks, modest API spend)

Two workload families (one verifiable: math/code; one sampled from production logs), pool of 8 small models, n ∈ {3,5,7}, 1,500 items, strong model + strong-SC controls. Measure: accuracy at matched $, ρ_e, agreement-AUROC, risk–coverage AURC, paraphrase flip rate, P(all wrong). Fit the beta-binomial predictor, verify it against observed majority accuracy, and ship the cascade operating point.

**Bottom line**: consensus beats single strong judgment through exactly four mechanisms — variance reduction on stochastic tasks, cancellation of decorrelated errors, calibrated abstention enabling cascades, and redundancy against correlated-outage/adversarial single points of failure. It loses when errors correlate, members are weak, the answer space defies voting, or the strong model could have spent the same budget on its own self-consistency. The entire measurement program above reduces to quantifying those five quantities — p, ρ_e, answer-space structure, the budget curve, and tail behavior — and the beta-binomial model turns them into a deploy/no-deploy decision you can make from a 1,000-item dev slice.
reasoning:
The user is asking me to design a rigorous measurement framework for comparing "quality-of-consensus" of a small-model flock (ensemble of small LLMs) versus a strong remote model on real workloads, and to characterize when consensus actually beats single strong judgment.

This is a hard research-design problem. Let me think about what's actually being asked:

1. **Setup**: A "flock" of small models (e.g., 7B-13B models, possibly heterogeneous) that reach some form of consensus (majority vote, weighted aggregation, debate, etc.) versus a single strong frontier model (e.g., GPT-4-class or Claude-class).

2. **Goal**: Design a measurement methodology for "quality of consensus" — not just accuracy, but the quality properties of the consensus process itself: calibration, diversity, agreement dynamics, robustness, cost-efficiency, etc. And then determine empirically when the flock beats the strong model.

Let me think deeply about what "quality-of-consensus" means and how to measure it properly.

## Core conceptual framing

First, I need to distinguish several things often conflated:
- **Consensus mechanism** (how the flock aggregates: majority vote, Borda, weighted log-prob averaging, debate-and-revise, judge-model arbitration, MBR decoding / minimum Bayes risk, self-consistency)
- **Consensus outcome** (the final answer produced)
- **Consensus quality** (properties of both the process and the outcome)

Key insight from ensemble theory: ensembles beat individuals when (a) individual members are better than chance, (b) their errors are decorrelated, and (c) aggregation is appropriate to the answer structure. Condorcet jury theorem gives the classic result: if each voter is correct with probability p > 0.5 and votes are independent, majority accuracy → 1 as n grows. But LLM errors are NOT independent — they're correlated through shared training data, shared failure modes (e.g., all models fail on the same arithmetic slip), and shared prompt-induced biases. So the empirical question is precisely: how much error correlation is there, and does it kill the Condorcet advantage?

Also key: the comparison must be **cost-matched or explicitly cost-parameterized**, otherwise it's meaningless. A flock of 10 small models costs roughly comparable inference compute to one strong model call (or more). The honest comparison is at iso-compute, iso-latency, iso-dollar, and also the full Pareto frontier.

## What workloads?

Real workloads should span the axes where theory predicts different outcomes:
1. **Verifiable-answer tasks**: math (GSM8K, MATH, competition math), code generation (HumanEval+, SWE-bench-lite execution-checked), factual QA with exact answers (TriviaQA, NQ). These allow unambiguous scoring.
2. **Long-form/open-ended tasks**: summarization, writing, open-domain reasoning. Consensus is ill-defined here — need special handling (this is where consensus usually fails or needs pairwise-judge aggregation).
3. **Classification/selection tasks**: multiple-choice (MMLU), routing decisions, safety classification. Pure voting regime.
4. **Calibration-sensitive tasks**: medical triage-ish, risk assessment where confidence matters.
5. **Adversarial/distribution-shift slices**: perturbed inputs, out-of-distribution phrasings, long-tail topics. This is where flocks might shine (variance reduction) or fail (shared blind spots).
6. **Tasks with partial credit / structured outputs**: extraction, JSON schema adherence, multi-step agentic traces.

Important: real workloads means not just static benchmarks but production traffic samples — logged queries from an actual deployment, stratified.

## Defining "quality of consensus" — the measurement dimensions

I should propose a multi-dimensional metric suite:

### A. Outcome quality
1. **Accuracy/task success** per workload, with CIs via bootstrap over items AND over flocks (resample which models are in the flock — this is crucial; most papers report one flock composition).
2. **Cost-normalized quality**: accuracy per dollar, per token, per second. Pareto frontier analysis.
3. **Tail behavior**: P(fail | item is in hardest decile), worst-case regret vs best member. Consensus can help the mean but hurt the tail if errors correlate (all agree on wrong answer confidently).

### B. Process/aggregation quality
4. **Error correlation structure**: estimate pairwise error correlation φ between members (e.g., Cohen's kappa on correctness indicators, or phi coefficient). Build the "error covariance matrix." Predict ensemble gain from average correlation: for n members with accuracy p and average pairwise error correlation ρ_e, majority-vote accuracy has a known approximation. Actually let me think about the formula.

For binary outcomes with exchangeable voters, correct probability p, and equicorrelated errors: Let q = 1-p be error rate. If errors are equicorrelated with correlation ρ among error indicators, then P(majority correct) can be computed via the beta-binomial: the number of errors follows a beta-binomial(n, α, β) where the intra-class correlation is ρ = 1/(α+β+1)... Let me recall: beta-binomial with parameters (n, α, β) has variance np(1-p)[1 + (n-1)ρ] where p = α/(α+β) and ρ = 1/(α+β+1). So given measured p̂ and ρ̂, set α+β = 1/ρ - 1, α = p(1/ρ - 1), β = (1-p)(1/ρ - 1). Then majority-wrong probability = P(X > n/2) where X ~ BetaBinomial(n, α, β) counting errors. That's a clean, practical estimator. Good — I'll include this.

5. **Diversity decomposition**: decompose ensemble error into bias/variance/ambiguity terms (Kohavi-Wolpert style, or the "bias-variance-covariance decomposition" for ensembles). For regression-style scoring: E[(f̄ - y)²] = bias² + avg variance + avg covariance... For classification use the Disagreement/Ambiguity decomposition.

6. **Agreement-vs-accuracy calibration curve**: plot P(correct | flock agreement level k/n). A good flock shows monotone relationship; miscalibration here means agreement is not informative. Measure AUROC of agreement as predictor of correctness. Also compare against the strong model's self-reported confidence AUROC. If agreement-AUROC > confidence-AUROC, you have a useful abstention signal.

7. **Consensus stability / fragility**: 
   - Resampling stability: bootstrap over which n members form the flock; report distribution of accuracy (std across compositions).
   - Prompt-perturbation sensitivity: paraphrase prompts, measure flip rate of consensus answer vs strong model's flip rate.
   - Order/format sensitivity for structured outputs.
   - Leave-one-out sensitivity: how much does removing one member change the answer? High LOO volatility = fragile consensus.

8. **Abstention/selective prediction**: with consensus, you get natural abstention (low agreement → abstain). Plot risk-coverage curves: selective accuracy vs coverage for flock-consensus-with-abstention vs strong-model-with-confidence-threshold. This is one of the strongest practical arguments for flocks: not raw accuracy but *selective* accuracy at matched coverage. Compute AURC (area under risk-coverage curve).

9. **Honesty of disagreement**: when members disagree, is the minority ever right? Measure "minority signal value": P(minority correct) and whether a learned aggregator (weighted vote trained on dev set) beats simple majority. Gap between majority vote and learned stacking = headroom left on the table by naive consensus.

### C. Economic/systems dimensions
10. Cost accounting: dollars, tokens (input/output separately since caching differs), wall-clock latency (p50/p95 — flock can parallelize so latency may be fine even at high token count), energy maybe.
11. Failure modes under degradation: rate-limit one provider, add latency jitter, kill a member — graceful degradation curve. Flock degrades gracefully; single strong model has cliff risk. This matters for production.
12. Data contamination audit: check benchmark overlap for both flock members and strong model (canary strings, n-gram overlap). Contamination inflates strong-model numbers on public benchmarks; real-workload eval avoids this.

### D. Statistical rigor
13. Paired comparisons: same items to both systems; McNemar's test for binary outcomes, paired bootstrap for continuous scores. Report effect sizes with CIs, not just p-values.
14. Multiple-comparison correction across workloads (Benjamini-Hochberg).
15. Power analysis: how many items needed to detect a 2-point accuracy gap? With paired designs and item-level correlation, typically need ~2-5k items for ±1.5% CI at 95%. Give concrete numbers.
16. Pre-registration of metrics and slicing to avoid garden-of-forking-paths.

## Consensus mechanisms to test (the flock side)

Need to test multiple aggregators because "consensus" is not one thing:
1. **Self-consistency within one small model** (sample k times, majority vote) — baseline that isolates "sampling diversity" from "model diversity."
2. **Cross-model majority vote** (heterogeneous flock).
3. **Weighted vote** (weights from dev-set performance or logprob-based).
4. **MBR (minimum Bayes risk) decoding**: pick the candidate answer with max average similarity/utility to all other candidates. Better than exact-match voting for free-form text.
5. **Debate protocols**: rounds of critique/revision, then final vote. Measures: convergence rate, sycophancy drift (do weaker models drag down stronger ones? measure pre/post debate accuracy per member), token cost multiplier.
6. **Judge/arbitrator**: small models propose + vote, a mid-tier model adjudicates disagreements only (cascade). 
7. **Cascade/deferral**: strong model only handles items where flock disagrees or flock confidence low. This is the "consensus as router" pattern — often the actual winner in practice.

For each mechanism, record: accuracy, cost, latency, calibration of the resulting decision, and sensitivity to hyperparameters (k samples, threshold).

## The strong-model baselines

Not just one call:
- Single greedy call (standard).
- Self-consistency on the strong model (k samples, majority) — CRITICAL baseline. Much of the flock's gain evaporates when the strong model also gets k-sample self-consistency at matched budget. This is the honest control most demos skip.
- Strong model with extended thinking/budget forcing if available.
- Fine-tuned/distilled small model as another control (distillation is the alternative way to spend the same money).

Budget matching: define budget units in $ per item; sweep budget; plot accuracy-vs-budget curves for (a) flock, (b) strong single, (c) strong SC, (d) cascade. The claim "consensus beats strong judgment" must hold at matched budget points on the curve, ideally with CIs on the curves.

## When does consensus actually win? Hypotheses to test (theory-driven)

From ensemble theory + known LLM failure structure:

Wins expected when:
1. **High item-level variance, low error correlation**: tasks where small models are stochastic (long CoT with branching, code with many valid implementations, retrieval-dependent QA where each model retrieves differently). Diversity sources: different pretraining data, different tool access, different temperatures/prompts/personas.
2. **Answer space is discrete/small**: MCQ, short-form factoid, unit tests pass/fail. Voting well-defined. For free text, need MBR/judge — quality drops.
3. **Per-item difficulty heterogeneity + measurable agreement**: enables selective prediction and cascades; big wins in risk-adjusted terms even when raw accuracy ties.
4. **Errors are idiosyncratic rather than systematic**: e.g., arithmetic slips, hallucinated entity names differ across models; but shared misconceptions (both flunk the same trick question) don't cancel.
5. **Strong model is contaminated/miscalibrated on the slice** while flock members err independently — e.g., memorized-but-wrong patterns.
6. **Latency-parallelizable settings** where 10 parallel calls ≈ 1 call latency.
7. **Availability/robustness requirements**: no single point of failure.

Losses expected when:
1. **Correlated failures**: shared tokenizer/training-data biases, adversarial inputs that exploit common architectures, subtle reasoning traps everyone falls for. Measure: conditional P(all wrong | any wrong) — the "common-mode failure rate."
2. **Long-form generation**: no canonical answer space; voting degenerates; judge models introduce their own bias; MBR converges to bland mode-seeking output (quality drop on creative/diverse tasks).
3. **Reasoning depth asymmetry**: tasks requiring a capability gap larger than what voting recovers — if strong model is 90% and flock members are 55% with high correlation, majority is worse. Condorcet requires p>0.5 per member AND independence; below-chance members actively hurt (need inverse weighting or exclusion).
4. **Sequential/stateful tasks**: agentic multi-step where errors compound; consensus per-step doesn't fix trajectory-level divergence; cost explodes.
5. **Strict latency SLOs with large outputs**.
6. **When the strong model's self-consistency closes the gap** — i.e., much of the flock benefit is just "ensembling," which the strong model can buy too.

Quantitative decision rule: derive from the beta-binomial model — flock majority beats strong single iff P(BetaBin majority correct) > p_strong. Given measured (p_flock_member, ρ_e, n), you can predict this before running everything; use as a screening tool, validate empirically. Also give the crossover condition in closed form for the equicorrelated case.

Let me actually derive the equicorrelated majority formula concretely so the answer contains something usable.

Beta-binomial: X ~ BB(n, α, β), P(X=k) = C(n,k) B(k+α, n-k+β)/B(α,β). Mean np, variance np(1-p)[1+(n-1)ρ] with ρ = 1/(α+β+1). So given member error rate q=1-p and error correlation ρ: α+β = (1-ρ)/ρ, α = q(1-ρ)/ρ, β = p(1-ρ)/ρ. Majority wrong = P(X ≥ ⌈n/2⌉+... ) careful with tie-breaking: for odd n, majority wrong = P(X > n/2) = P(X ≥ (n+1)/2). For even n, define tie policy (random tie-break → count half).

Example: n=7, p=0.7 (q=0.3), ρ=0.1: α+β=9, α=2.7, β=6.3. P(X≥4) where X~BB(7,2.7,6.3). Rough numeric: independent case would give P(wrong majority)=P(Bin(7,0.3)≥4)= 35*.3^4*.7^3 + 21*.3^5*.7^2 + 7*.3^6*.7 + .3^7 = 35*0.0081*0.343=0.0972; 21*0.00243*0.49=0.02505; 7*0.000729*0.7=0.00357; 0.0002187 → total ≈ 0.126. So majority correct ≈ 87.4% vs single 70%. With ρ=0.1 the effective variance inflation factor is 1+(n-1)ρ = 1.6, pushing P(wrong majority) up to maybe ~0.17-0.18 → ~82-83% correct. Still above 70%. With ρ=0.3: variance factor 2.8; P(wrong majority) maybe ~0.24 → 76%. With ρ=0.5: factor 4 → ~72%, barely better than single. So the rule of thumb: with n=7 members at 70% each, you need average error correlation below ~0.4-0.5 to beat a 90% strong model? No wait — 83% < 90%. To beat a 90% strong model with 70%-accurate members you'd need very low ρ and larger n. At ρ=0.1, n=21: variance factor 3.0, sd of error fraction = sqrt(qp*(1+(n-1)ρ)/n) = sqrt(.21*3/21)=sqrt(.03)=0.173; z=(0.5-0.3)/0.173≈1.155 → P(wrong majority)≈12.4% → 87.6% correct. Hmm still below 90. n=41, ρ=0.05: factor 3.0, sd=sqrt(.21*3/41)=sqrt(.01537)=0.124; z=1.61→ 5.4% wrong → 94.6%. So ~40 members at 70% with ρ=0.05 beats a 90% model. That's the honest math showing why flocks rarely beat frontier models on raw accuracy — they win on cost-adjusted, calibrated-selective, and robustness grounds instead. I should include this kind of worked example because it makes the framework quantitative.

Actually, let me double-check the normal approx usage for beta-binomial tails — fine for illustration purposes; note it's approximate and recommend exact computation via the beta-binomial PMF in practice.

Also worth including: the "diversity dividend" identity. For probabilistic classifiers, ensemble squared error = average member squared error − diversity (ambiguity). Krogh & Vedelsby: E_ens = Ē − D where D is weighted variance of member outputs around ensemble mean. Non-negative diversity ⇒ ensemble never worse than average member (for squared loss, linear averaging). But majority voting isn't averaging; and for 0-1 loss the guarantee is weaker. Worth stating precisely to avoid hand-waving.

Another key measurement: **oracle gaps**.
- Majority-of-flock vs oracle-any-member (pick best member per item): huge gap = headroom for learned selection/routing.
- Oracle-best-of-k-samples for strong model similarly.
- These gaps tell you whether the ceiling is aggregation-limited or member-limited.

And **per-slice analysis**: stratify by difficulty (strong-model correctness as proxy or IRT difficulty), topic cluster (embeddings), input length, language, format. Consensus gains concentrate in specific slices; report per-slice deltas with shrinkage (empirical Bayes) to avoid noise-chasing.

## Experimental design specifics

- Items: N ≈ 3–10k per workload family for tight CIs; paired design.
- Flock compositions: sample M random flocks of size n ∈ {3,5,7,11} from a pool of P small models (P ≥ 20 across families/sizes/providers) to get composition-variance CIs. Report mean ± std across compositions, plus min/max.
- Sampling params: temperature fixed per protocol (e.g., T=0.7 for SC sampling); record seeds; run each member once per item for cross-model vote (or k samples for within-model SC).
- Answer normalization/extraction: deterministic extractor per task; exact-match grading where possible; model-grader only for open-ended, with grader validated against human labels on a 200-item subset (report grader-human agreement κ ≥ 0.8 required).
- Human eval subset: 300–500 items stratified, double-annotated, for open-ended quality (win-rate with expert judges, blind pairwise).
- Leakage controls: private held-out sets built fresh; canary insertion; timestamp-bounded tasks (problems created after model cutoffs) as contamination-free slice.
- Compute ledger: log every call's tokens/$/latency; normalize $ using list prices at eval time; also report token-equivalent compute.
- Pre-register primary metric: e.g., "accuracy at $X/item" and "AURC"; secondary: tail risk, robustness deltas.

## Decision framework: when to deploy flock vs strong

Output a decision procedure:
1. Estimate (p_i, ρ_e) cheaply on a dev slice (500–1000 items).
2. Predict majority accuracy via beta-binomial; compare to strong model at matched budget.
3. Check answer-space discreteness; if free-form, plan MBR/judge and expect smaller gains.
4. Check latency SLO and parallelism feasibility.
5. Check tail-risk requirements: if worst-case matters, prefer flock+cascade (abstain/defer on disagreement).
6. Deploy pattern recommendation table: 
   - Cheap high-volume discrete tasks → flock vote (+cascade to strong on disagreement): likely winner on cost-quality.
   - Hard reasoning → strong model (possibly with SC); flock only as verifier/critic panel.
   - Open-ended creation → strong single; flock for rubric-based review ensemble (judge panel reduces grader variance — different role: consensus as evaluator, not generator).
   - Safety-critical → flock for detection redundancy + strong for resolution; measure false-negative correlation explicitly (two models both missing a violation is the dangerous event; measure P(both miss)).

That last point deserves emphasis: in moderation/safety, the relevant metric is P(joint miss) which is exactly the common-mode failure measurement. Flock value proposition = reducing joint-miss probability when errors decorrelate.

## Metrics formulas to include

- Pairwise error correlation: φ = (P(both wrong) − q_i q_j)/sqrt(q_i(1−q_i)q_j(1−q_j)); average over pairs → ρ_e.
- Predicted majority accuracy via beta-binomial with (q̄, ρ_e, n).
- Diversity dividend (regression tasks): D = E_i w_i (f_i − f̄)²; E_ens = Ē_bias² ... keep simple: report Ē − E_ens as realized diversity dividend.
- Agreement-AUROC; risk-coverage AURC; ECE of agreement-derived confidence (fit isotonic on dev).
- Flip rate under paraphrase (consensus vs strong).
- Common-mode failure rate: P(all members wrong | at least one wrong) and unconditional P(all wrong).
- Cost-quality frontier AUC or accuracy at fixed budget points {1x, 3x, 10x} relative to strong-single-call price.
- Graceful degradation: accuracy vs fraction of members dropped (simulate outages).

## Pitfalls section

- Comparing flock-of-10-cost to single-call-cost (budget mismatch) — the #1 flaw.
- Not running strong-model self-consistency control.
- One flock composition, treating members as interchangeable.
- Grading open-ended outputs with the same strong model that's a competitor (judge bias) — use blind pairwise with position swap, multiple graders, human anchor.
- Item selection effects (benchmark contamination).
- Ignoring tie-breaking and answer-extraction losses in voting.
- Reporting means without composition variance.
- Correlation estimated on easy items only (restriction of range inflates apparent independence... actually on easy items everyone is right, errors rare → correlation estimates unstable; need stratified estimation on medium/hard slices).
- Temperature confounds: flock diversity from temperature vs genuine model diversity — ablate.
- Latency measured naively: parallel calls share rate limits; measure end-to-end under concurrency.

Also the reverse cascade: strong proposes, flock verifies (critique panel). Measure catch rate of flock on strong-model errors: P(≥1 member flags | strong wrong) vs false-alarm rate. Open-ended tasks: define quality via (a) blind pairwise win-rate vs strong reference judged by panel of graders + humans; (b) rubric score. Now the "when consensus beats" summary — I want a crisp table:

| Condition | Flock favored when | Strong favored when |
- Member accuracy: >60–65% and reasonably homogeneous | <55% or highly skewed
- Error correlation: ρ_e < ~0.2–0.3 | ρ_e > 0.4 (common-mode failures dominate)
- Answer space: discrete/verifiable | free-form creative
- Budget: price ratio strong:flock ≥ n× (or cascade) | budget allows strong anyway
- Latency: parallelizable, loose p95 | strict single-call SLO
- Risk posture: need abstention/tail control | need best-mean quality
- Distribution shift: high variance regimes | stable in-distribution
- Adversarial: diverse architectures reduce transfer of attacks | targeted attacks on known stack
- Stateful agents: per-step voting insufficient | strong trajectory

And the punchline: consensus beats single strong judgment mainly through four mechanisms — (1) variance reduction on stochastic tasks, (2) decorrelated-error cancellation, (3) calibrated abstention enabling cascades, (4) redundancy against outage/adversarial single-points-of-failure. It loses when errors correlate, when the answer space defies voting, when members are weak, or when the strong model could have bought the same ensembling with its own budget. The measurement framework exists to quantify exactly those five things: p, ρ_e, answer-space structure, budget curve, and tail behavior.
